title: In Praise of the Unfinished Manuscript
script: Narrator: [wry] Somewhere in a drawer I no longer open sits a manuscript I abandoned at two hundred pages, a book on translation theory that I once believed would justify an entire decade of study.
Narrator: [reflective] For years I treated its incompletion as a private scandal, evidence submitted quietly against my own competence whenever self-doubt required fresh material.

Narrator: [thoughtful] It was only recently, rereading a stranger's memoir on failed ambitions, that I encountered a phrase that reorganized my entire relationship to that drawer: the unfinished work as apprenticeship rather than epitaph.

Narrator: [candid] I had assumed, with the tidy arrogance of the newly credentialed, that scholarship accrued linearly, each finished project a rung toward some eventual mastery I'd recognize on arrival.

Narrator: [wry] Nobody warns you that the arrival is largely fictional, that even accomplished scholars are mostly improvising atop earlier improvisations, several of which they'd rather nobody excavate.

Narrator: [honest] What that abandoned manuscript actually taught me, in retrospect, wasn't translation theory at all but the far more useful skill of recognizing when an argument has quietly stopped believing in itself.

Narrator: [reflective] I couldn't finish the book because, somewhere around page one hundred and fifty, I'd stopped agreeing with my own premise, and no amount of stubbornness could resurrect a conviction I no longer held.
Narrator: [wry] Better, surely, to abandon a manuscript honestly than to complete one dishonestly, however unglamorous the former looks on a curriculum vitae.

Narrator: [warmly] These days, when younger colleagues confess to a drawer of their own, half-finished and faintly embarrassing, I tell them what I wish someone had told me: the drawer isn't a graveyard.

Narrator: [with quiet conviction] It's closer to a ledger of every conviction you were honest enough to abandon once it stopped being true, which strikes me now as considerably more respectable than never having doubted anything at all.
